opening_note: A short, demo-led student presentation: explain one joint and two PPO policies, run the actual code, show the generated graphs and results, then connect the finding to the readings and a robotics application. Suggested duration is about five to six minutes including a 60–90 second code demonstration. The included figures are verified cloud results; clearly identify any new local results. Success remains a full five-second episode with RMSE < 0.32 rad and no safety termination. The main program retrains and replaces its generated outputs; the optional saved-model replay preserves them.

slides.title: What am I demonstrating?
slides.cue: Can training with varied physics help a joint controller handle an unfamiliar environment?
slides.script: My project tests whether varied training physics improves a learned controller's robustness. I model one robotic joint, where a PPO policy chooses a target angle and a PD controller supplies the torque. One policy trains with fixed physics; the other experiences randomized inertia, friction, and delay. I compare their joint tracking in nominal and unfamiliar simulations.
slides.point_to: Point to the single joint, the fixed-physics policy, and the randomized-physics policy.
slides.transition: I will run the program and briefly show where that comparison happens.

slides.title: Run the code and follow the workflow
slides.cue: The program builds the joint, trains two policies, evaluates both, and saves the graphs.
slides.script: I run reading5_sim2real_ppo.py using the project's Python environment. In Joint.step, the policy's angle target becomes a saturated PD torque, then the joint dynamics advance. In train, Stable-Baselines3 PPO learns from tracking rewards. The main function checks the environment, trains both policies, evaluates thirty matched episodes per policy and condition, prints the metrics, and creates three graphs. The saved run took about twenty-eight seconds on the cloud CPU.
slides.point_to: Run .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe reading5_sim2real_ppo.py. Show Joint.step and train while it runs, then point to the terminal results and generated PNGs.

slides.title: Does the joint follow the target?
slides.cue: The dashed line is the desired angle; the colored line shows what the joint does.
slides.script: The terminal shows evaluation statistics, and the program also saves the training-reward graph. Here I focus on the held-out tracking plot. The dashed line is the desired angle; the colored line is the joint's actual angle. The randomized policy tracks more smoothly in this example. Both policies pass this seed, so overall success needs all thirty trials.

slides.title: What do the results mean?
slides.cue: Randomization improved held-out performance for this policy pair; both policies succeeded in nominal simulation.
slides.script: Both policies succeeded in all thirty nominal trials. In the unfamiliar simulation, the fixed policy succeeded in fourteen of thirty trials, compared with twenty-nine of thirty for the randomized policy. Mean tracking RMSE decreased from 0.3299 to 0.2250 radians. This supports better robustness for this trained policy pair, while one training seed and simplified physics limit the conclusion.
slides.point_to: Point to 14/30 versus 29/30, the held-out RMSE values, and the nominal 100% bars. Success requires RMSE below 0.32 rad for a full safe episode.
slides.transition: That result illustrates the sim-to-real ideas discussed in the assigned readings.

slides.title: How does this connect to Reading 5?
slides.cue: The readings connect randomized simulation, policy learning, and the gap between a model and a robot.
slides.script: Tan and colleagues motivate randomized simulation and careful actuator modeling for robot transfer. Zhao and colleagues place these methods within the broader reality-gap problem. Sutton and Barto explain policy-gradient foundations; PPO is the specific clipped-surrogate actor–critic method used here. MuJoCo represents richer multibody and contact simulation. My simple joint illustrates these ideas without reproducing full robot physics.
slides.point_to: Point to each source and its one-line connection. MuJoCo is a reference connection, not a dependency used by this program.
slides.transition: A practical application is a robot joint whose physical behavior changes during use.

slides.title: A real robotics application and the takeaway
slides.cue: Training across plausible variation may help controllers tolerate changing loads, friction, and actuator delays.
slides.script: In a quadruped inspired by Go2 or ANYmal, payload changes can alter effective joint inertia, wear can change friction, and communication can introduce delay. Randomized training is one way to prepare a controller for that variation. My result demonstrates this idea in simulation. It does not establish physical robot transfer, balance, or walking; those require richer models and hardware validation.
slides.point_to: Connect inertia to load, friction to wear, and latency to actuator communication. End with the measured held-out improvement and its simulation-only scope.

qa.question: Is this an actual physical sim-to-real experiment?
qa.short_answer: It compares two simulated conditions; no physical robot was tested.
qa.answer: The held-out environment is a simulated approximation of unfamiliar reality. It uses greater inertia, friction, delay, and sensor noise, but no calibrated robot or hardware trial. Physical transfer would require a realistic model, reliable sensing, protective limits, and supervised experiments.

qa.question: Why would domain randomization help?
qa.short_answer: It exposes the policy to varied dynamics during training.
qa.answer: Randomization reduces dependence on one exact training model by varying inertia, friction, and delay at each reset. It may encourage a controller that tolerates uncertainty. It is not guaranteed to help: the training range, learning budget, and held-out condition all affect the outcome.

qa.question: Why does PPO choose an angle instead of torque?
qa.short_answer: The learned target works through an understandable PD control loop.
qa.answer: PPO supplies a bounded target angle, while PD feedback converts the difference between target and measured state into torque. This separates the learned decision from a familiar actuator-control structure. Torque saturation is explicit, but this architecture alone does not prove closed-loop safety or stability.

qa.question: How does PPO differ from general policy-gradient methods?
qa.short_answer: PPO is one particular actor–critic policy-gradient algorithm.
qa.answer: Policy-gradient methods adjust policy parameters to improve expected return. PPO is a specific method that uses a clipped surrogate objective to discourage overly large policy updates, together with a learned value function. Sutton and Barto provide the broader foundations rather than this particular implementation.

qa.question: What do these results actually establish?
qa.short_answer: Randomization helped this policy pair in one held-out simulated condition.
qa.answer: The randomized policy achieved 29/30 held-out successes versus 14/30 for the fixed policy, with lower mean RMSE. Both had 30/30 nominal success. Only one training seed per policy was used, so this is a measured case study rather than a general superiority or hardware-transfer claim.

qa.question: How can I repeat the classroom demonstration?
qa.short_answer: Rerun the program, or replay saved policies without retraining.
qa.answer: The main program can be rerun and regenerates its outputs. For evaluation without retraining or replacing those files, use classroom/demo.py --trials 30 --rounds 1. Each helper launch gets a new folder. Reusing seeds checks execution repeatability, not additional independent evidence.
